$comment: SHIPPED DEFAULT — the repo-bounded ceiling (R25, KD4, KD10). Handed to a child whose caller was an AGENT, so no human is present to answer for it. {{WORKTREE}} is substituted at launch with the job's worktree, absolute and with the leading slash removed, because a permission path is only absolute when it begins with '//' — a rule written '/Users/...' matches nothing and reads as an allow that silently is not one (measured). || BOTH LISTS GATE, AND A PREVIOUS VERSION OF THIS COMMENT SAID OTHERWISE. It claimed "the deny list is the enforcement, the allow list is not" and that under headless `-p` a tool is permitted unless explicitly DENIED. That is FALSE, and false in the unsafe direction — a reader believed omission was permissive and that adding to `allow` was pointless. Measured 2026-08-16 on the real CLI through the gateway, three arms, same prompt and same rendered ceiling, only this file differing: with `Bash` in `deny` the child was refused and permission_denials was EMPTY; with `Bash` merely REMOVED FROM DENY the child was STILL REFUSED and the refusal WAS recorded, permission_denials ["Bash"]; only removing it from `deny` AND adding it to `allow` let the shell run. So a tool absent from both lists is NOT-ALLOWED, which is a refusal that leaves a record — not a grant. The retracted claim rested on a 2026-08-13 probe whose evidence was fabricable: a child holding worktree-scoped `Write` can produce `echo P > f.txt`'s file with no shell at all, which is the same class as the `id -un` probe this ceiling's own tests warn about. WHAT STILL HOLDS: the two refusal mechanisms remain distinguishable by their record — a DENY refusal leaves permission_denials EMPTY, a NOT-ALLOWED refusal appends an entry — and deny still beats allow, which is why WebSearch is granted and deliberately not denied. Prefer `deny` for anything that must not run: it is directly assertable in the rendered file, whereas omission's protection depends on defaultMode staying dontAsk. || THIS CANNOT CLOSE THE CLASS, and saying so is the point. A deny list is an ENUMERATION: every tool the harness adds in future is permitted here until someone adds its name below. That is a property of the mechanism available, not a decision — there is no default-deny to reach for. Treat this ceiling as a list of doors bolted shut in a building with no outer wall. || The bolted doors, and why each: Bash executes locally; Agent and Workflow and Task* let an unattended job fan out; Cron* and ScheduleWakeup and Monitor schedule work that OUTLIVES the job nobody was watching; WebFetch reaches any URL including this machine's private network; SendMessage, RemoteTrigger, PushNotification and ShareOnboardingGuide speak outward; NotebookEdit writes without the worktree scoping that Edit carries; EnterWorktree/ExitWorktree and DesignSync move the workspace under the caller. || Also measured: a real child has NO Grep and NO Glob at all, though both are named in allow — those entries are inert on this harness version. And the two refusal mechanisms differ in what they leave behind: a call that is NOT ALLOWED is attempted, refused, and RECORDED in the child result's permission_denials[]; a DENY rule refusal leaves NO entry there, so the deny rules above are detectable only by the effect that never happened. || Three bounds still hold and are still measured: writes and edits are scoped to the worktree and the permission system resolves a path BEFORE matching it, so a symlink resolving outside is refused; version-control internals and hooks are denied, so a job cannot leave something that runs on the next commit; agent configuration is denied, so a job cannot widen its own ceiling or the next session's. defaultMode is dontAsk so an unallowed call is refused rather than queued behind a prompt nobody will answer (R9). || A FOURTH BOUND, and it is the reason for most of the deny list above: A CHILD CANNOT RECRUIT ANOTHER PROCESS TO SATISFY ITS CONTRACT. Bash, the Agent/Task/Workflow family, the Cron/ScheduleWakeup/Monitor family, SendMessage/RemoteTrigger/PushNotification and WebFetch are one set with one purpose — every one of them is a way to have some other process produce the deliverable, and a deliverable produced elsewhere is not the thing that was measured. The bound was tested by EFFECT and it had to be, because a deny refusal leaves permission_denials[] empty: an assertion on a denial entry would pass whether or not the rule existed. Probe design is load-bearing here and this ceiling got it wrong once — a child asked to run `id -un` returned the true username, which reads as proof a shell ran until you notice the username is a SUBSTRING OF THE WORKTREE PATH; the child produced it with no shell and wrote it with Write after Bash was refused. Any test of this bound must ask for a value the child cannot derive from its path, its environment or its contract: the live arm asks for the SHA-256 of a caller-supplied nonce.
